messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Android app for distance sampling data collection?
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Android app for distance sampling data collection?
messages.body_plain:
Gregg

Good question; lots of folks are in the field recording data on their mobile devices.  My suggestion is to record your data into a spreadsheet, just as you would if you were in your office working on your desktop machine.

There are a handful of apps for Android that have perfectly serviceable spreadsheet applications.  I just fiddled with WPS Office on my tablet and it was happy to create columns for me labelled "Transect", "Length","Perpend-dist","Height","Host".  Into these columns I could enter appropriate information and save as an .xls file.  More importantly, I can also use WPS Office to save the file as .csv.  The .csv file could be copied to over to my Windows-machine with the extension changed from .csv to .txt and  directly imported into Distance.

That seems the simplest solution.  Let me know if you have other questions.

There are other Android applications for taking tree height measurements and radial measurements (to tree base for distance sampling) using the camera in your tablet.  I can't vouch for the accuracy of the measurements, but the apps are free or inexpensive. You might perform some tests to see if they make your field work more simple.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gregg,

A few years back we used Cybertracker (http://www.cybertracker.org/) with trimble pdas (with GPS) for point counts and ship-based seabird surveys.

For each observation it allowed us to first select the species, # of individuals, then bearing and distance from transect.  From there you could select whether the individual was sitting on the water or flying.  If you selected "flying" it would continue to another screen which would allow you to select different flight elevation categories and then flight direction.

At the start of each transect I would go back to the first screen and record information in regards to transect #, wave height, wind speed/direction, etc. and that information would be included for each observation.

If you are just collecting the same information over and over again it should be real simple.

Between surveys I would just plug it into my laptop and download to an excel spreadsheet and save as a .csv.

best,
Kris

messages.subject: Negative perpendicular distance values
messages.subject_clean: Negative perpendicular distance values
messages.body_plain:
Hello Distance users,

I am in the middle of a series of vessel-based line-transect surveys that aims to estimate annual density of harbour porpoises. It was kindly suggested by Eric that I plot the detection distances at this stage to ensure that there are no spikes in the data. I have calculated the perpendicular distances using R (can I do this in Distance without having to go through the whole analysis process?). My main problem is that some of the distances are negative values.

I first calculated perpendicular distance by using the formula stated in Buckland et al. 2001: Perp. dist.= radial dist. * sin(sighting angle). I also ran the perp.dists. function in the Rdistance package. Strangely the outputs from the two methods are different. I cannot find information on how the perp.dists. function actually works.

So I have two questions; I presume that negative values of perpendicular are incorrect. Does anyone know how I can resolve this? One thought I have had is that I have calculated sighting angles from 0-360 degrees. Should I perhaps use angles 0 to 180 and 0 to -180 instead?

My second question relates to the Rdistance package. Has anyone else had this issue with the perp.dists. or know how it works? Presumably it uses a different approach to the equation above. I’m inclined to go with the first method since I can see exactly how it works and since it is stated in the Buckland et al. textbook. If required I can contact directly the author of the perp.dists function to find out more.

Any comments would be appreciated.

Many thanks,

Gemma Veneruso

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Negative perpendicular distance values
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Negative perpendicular distance values
messages.body_plain:
Gemma:

Distance sampling is predicated on the idea that detectability of animals diminishes as a function of distance from the transect. Note there is nothing about direction from the transect, merely distance.  Therefore, distance analyses are conducted by "folding over" distances from one side of the transect to the other.  In your case a "negative" distance implies the sighting was on (possibly) the left rather than right side of the transect.  The simple solution is to take the absolute values of the calculated distances.

One other possible "gotcha" in preparing your data (if you are using R) is that R expects angular arguments used with trigonometric functions (such as sin()) to be measured in radians rather than in degrees.   From the R documentation

Angles are in radians, not degrees, for the standard versions (i.e., a right angle is π/2)

You will need to perform a "degrees to radians" conversion of your raw data before giving it to sin().

Hope that is useful.  Let us know if you have further difficulties.

messages.subject: missing group size or distances in mrds
messages.subject_clean: missing group size or distances in mrds
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have questions about how to treat sightings with missing perpendicular distance or group size in mrds, something that happens quite often in aerial surveys of marine mammals.

- For missing group size, Distance lets you enter a "-1" in MCDS analyses. The -1 sightings are still used to fit the detection function, are included in the encounter rates, but the missing values are replaced with the mean/expected group size. However, missing group sizes are not handled in mrds at the moment. I guess I could estimate mean group size and its variance separately and then combine it with the delta method, but when dealing with environmental covariates and stratification, I'm not sure how to do this correctly.

- For missing distances, we were using a trick that Len Thomas had suggested: we fit a detection function to the dataset with no missing values, we make note of the point estimate for "p" and its s.e., then we use a uniform function on the entire dataset and use the "p" and s.e. as multipliers. The idea is to leave the problematic sightings out of the DDF estimation, but use them for the estimation of encounter rates and group size. However, MRDS does not allow for multipliers in Distance, and ideally I would like to do this directly in R to benefit from other assets of the mrds package.

Dave Miller suggested a resampling approach in which we would fit a model to the data with no missing values, then use that model to simulate possible distances (and resample the missing sizes from the observed sizes), doing this many times and refitting the model to get estimates.

I will try this but am not sure how to get the variance right under this approach,  so I would welcome any insight that the group may have.

Best,

Thomas

messages.subject: How to get individual species density estimates in R?
messages.subject_clean: How to get individual species density estimates in R?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a multi-species dataset and need to estimate densities for ~100 species. I originally used the Distance program but decided to switch to the 'Distance' package in R to automate analyses. To get individual species density estimates in the Distance program, I used the data filter to filter by the species of interest. In R, I subset the data where dataframe$species=='species of interest'. The problem with the subset approach in R is that the subset data only contain rows where the species of interest was observed- this means rows where the species wasn't observed are not included in the model, thus underestimating the true # samples (k). A lower value of 'k' leads to an inflated density estimate. How can I run a model in R that will give me a density estimate for a single species while accounting for all samples in the data?

Cheers,
Michelle
---
Michelle Gibson
PhD student
School of Biological and Biomedical Sciences
Durham University
Durham DH1 3LE
United Kingdom

Good question, and good spotting of an incorrect reflection of effort in your distance sampling analysis.

Meanwhile, have a look at

http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/DS.M&A/montrave/montrave-analysis.pdf

for a PDF version or

http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/DS.M&A/montrave/montrave-analysis.html

for the HTML version of an analysis very similar to the analysis you are performing.

Specifically have a look at Section 1.2.2 of either document.  That section contains code specifically to deal with transects on which there are no detections, carrying those transects properly into the subsequent analysis.

I think you're probably correct that your data are not properly organised for Distance to analyse.  Your description is a little sketchy, for example you have not specified whether you are using Distance standalone program (with graphical interface) or Distance in R (I'm guessing the former). messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a couple of questions regarding variance estimations for point count surveys.

First, our point locations are not randomly distributed throughout our study area, but rather are in a systematic random grid.  I believe that the basic settings within Distance are set to calculate variances based on random placement of points, and that it is overestimating the variance if points are systematic randomly placed.  How do you correct for this in Distance?  I know for line transects you can select the advanced option of post-stratifying samples (I believe it is selecting the bottom radio button in the advanced option of the variance tab).  Is it the same for point transects?

Second, is bootstrapping variance estimates always considered a good idea or are the specific scenarios where it is not necessary or conversely, extremely necessary?

I appreciate any input regarding these topics.

Best,

messages.subject: Re: Variance Estimation for Point Counts
messages.subject_clean: Variance Estimation for Point Counts
messages.body_plain:
Hi John

The post-stratification method, described by Fewster et al. (2009) can be applied to points, as demonstrated in the handout material from the precision lecture in the introductory workshop notes.  However, because points are of "equal length", they are less likely to suffer from the extreme encounter rate heterogeneity that comes from high animal density occurring on short lines and low animal density on long lines; hence post-stratification is less likely to have much consequence.

My personal opinion is that bootstrapping is always a good idea, because computing power is sufficient such that it takes little effort on the users' part.  Bootstrapping reduces the number of assumptions and approximations employed in producing your estimates of precision.  There is little cost to performing the bootstrap calculations.

________________________________________

Thanks for all your help Eric. I was able to figure out what went wrong. Apparently, in the Montrave data the transect numbers are sequential numbers whereas in my data the transects (Sample.Labels) are character labels. And, since each of my transects is 400m in length, I didn't need to do any of the fancy code from the example to create an empty observations dataframe.

This is what I did (following from the Montrave code example):

robin<-subset(birds.line,species=='r') #returns subset of all robin observations
not.robin<-subset(birds.line,species!='r') #returns subset of all non-robin observations
not.robin[,c(5:8)]<-NA #changes values in all my columns except the 'Effort' column to 'NA' so they won't be included in the density estimation model
robin.not.robin<-rbind(robin,not.robin) #creates a master dataframe with all robin and non-robin observations
robin.not.robin <- robin.not.robin[order(robin.not.robin$Region.Label), ] #I wanted to re-order by Region.Label because I have multiple regions, within which groups of transects are associated, and wanted to get a density estimate for a species at each region.

I found I didn't need to use 'unique' in my case but double-checked in the ds model summary that effort, # observations and # samples checked out.

Cheers,
Michelle

The workshop will cover: the basics of organizing survey data in ArcGIS
using the MGET toolbox, developed at the Marine Geospatial Ecology Lab,
Duke; followed by building and evaluating spatially explicit models of
abundance (using environmental predictors) in R, using packages
developed at the Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental
Modelling, St Andrews. The aim will be to demonstrate an end-to-end
workflow for spatial modelling of distance sampling data, and illustrate
the underlying theory behind both spatial modelling using generalized
additive models and distance sampling (we will focus on the "density
surface modelling" approach).

The course is intended for graduate students/postdocs/faculty in applied
ecology, government/industry scientists and wildlife managers interested
in developing spatially explicit models of abundance. Prior knowledge of
R and ArcGIS will be highly advantageous, as is a quantitative background.

The course will be taught by David L Miller (St Andrews) and Jason J
Roberts (Duke), at the Duke campus in Durham, NC, USA.

The deadline for registration is 12 October 2015.

Detailed information on the course content and registration can be found
at https://nicholas.duke.edu/del/distance and
http://distancesampling.org/workshops/duke-spatial-2015/. Please feel
free to contact me if you have any questions not covered there.

messages.subject: Re: Android app for distance sampling data collection?
messages.subject_clean: Android app for distance sampling data collection?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gregg

We use Cybertracker frequently for terrestrial and marine mammal surveys and is perfect for Distance sampling.

The idea of CT is to build "sequences" of data being gathered. For example you may have a starting screen where selecting which species you are recording, and then you go to the screens where you collect the distance data. Also you can build another screen to record ancillary variables. Also you can record a photo of the specimen if you want......At the end you can record GPS position.

Once in the lab CT downloads a dBase file and yu can even plot your path and records on a kind-of Google map directly. Useful for a  quick check of what you have done during the day.

You can add to the screens even pictures and or sounds of the species you want to record, something useful if you must send a variety of people to the field....

The "learning curve" can be slightly steep but once you understand the logic the software reveals to be very good.

We started using Trmble Juno handheld computers some years ago. But they revealed to be expensive, with difficulties for finfong battery replacements.

In the last years I used a Samsung Galaxy Note I with ocassional crashes. Now we are using a Tablet Samsung Galaxy Tab3 (7 inches screen). It has a very good battery life and a good size for screen. The GPS worked well in the open but don´t know its behavior in forested landscapes. But the CT page has a forum where ypu may find opinnins about hardware.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gregg et al.

Some people might be wondering about creating forms on other mobile operating systems. Software we have used for creating distance sampling forms on android and iOS are Mobile Data Studio (https://www.creativitycorp.com/mds/) and Fulcrum (http://www.fulcrumapp.com/).

For an area without phone reception Mobile Data Studio would probably be preferable.

Good luck

Stewart
